extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of classic literature and moral aphorisms
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of aphoristic moral maxims (La Rochefoucauld) presented as concise reflections on human motives, passions, and social behavior. The page is a translated selection of numbered maxims with occasional editorial notes and short commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. What we term virtue is often but a mass of various actions
rubrics_metrics.description: What we term virtue is often but a mass of various actions and divers interests, which fortune, or our own industry, manage to arrange; and it is not always from valour or from chastity that men are brave, and women chaste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Who combats bravely is not therefore brave, He dreads a death-bed like the meanest slave; Who reasons wisely is not therefore wise, His pride in reasoning, not in acting, lies." Pope, Moral Essays, Ep. i. line 115.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Self-love is the greatest of flatterers
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-love is the greatest of flatterers.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Much of self-love remains unexplored
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever discoveries have been made in the region of self-love, there remain many unexplored territories there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [This is the first hint of the system the author tries to develope. He wishes to find in vice a motive for all our actions, but this does not suffice him; he is obliged to call other passions to the help of his system and to confound pride, vanity, interest and egotism with self love. This confusion destroys the unity of his principle.--Aime Martin.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. Self love is more cunning than the most cunning man
rubrics_metrics.description: Self love is more cunning than the most cunning man in the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Duration of passions not dependent on us
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of our passions is no more dependant upon us than the duration of our life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [Then what becomes of free will?--Aime; Martin]

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Passion renders clever men fools and fools clever
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion often renders the most clever man a fool, and even sometimes renders the most foolish man clever.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Great actions often caused by temper and passions not design
rubrics_metrics.description: Great and striking actions which dazzle the eyes are represented by politicians as the effect of great designs, instead of which they are commonly caused by the temper and the passions. Thus the war between Augustus and Anthony, which is set down to the ambition they entertained of making themselves masters of the world, was probably but an effect of jealousy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Passions are infallible advocates
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions are the only advocates which always persuade. They are a natural art, the rules of which are infallible; and the simplest man with passion will be more persuasive than the most eloquent without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [See Maxim 249 which is an illustration of this.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Passions possess injustice and self-interest; distrust them
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions possess a certain injustice and self interest which makes it dangerous to follow them, and in reality we should distrust them even when they appear most trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Human heart perpetually generates passions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the human heart there is a perpetual generation of passions; so that the ruin of one is almost always the foundation of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Passions often produce their contraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions often produce their contraries: avarice sometimes leads to prodigality, and prodigality to avarice; we are often obstinate through weakness and daring though timidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Care to conceal passions futile; they show through veils
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever care we take to conceal our passions under the appearances of piety and honour, they are always to be seen through these veils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The 1st edition, 1665, preserves the image perhaps better--"however we may conceal our passions under the veil, etc., there is always some place where they peep out."]

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Self love endures condemnation of tastes less than opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Our self love endures more impatiently the condemnation of our tastes than of our opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Men forget benefits and injuries; hate those who obliged them
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are not only prone to forget benefits and injuries; they even hate those who have obliged them, and cease to hate those who have injured them. The necessity of revenging an injury or of recompensing a benefit seems a slavery to which they are unwilling to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Clemency of princes often policy to win affection
rubrics_metrics.description: The clemency of Princes is often but policy to win the affections of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["So many are the advantages which monarchs gain by clemency, so greatly does it raise their fame and endear them to their subjects, that it is generally happy for them to have an opportunity of displaying it."--Montesquieu, Esprit Des Lois, Lib. VI., C. 21.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Clemency arises from vanity, idleness, fear
rubrics_metrics.description: This clemency of which they make a merit, arises oftentimes from vanity, sometimes from idleness, oftentimes from fear, and almost always from all three combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [La Rochefoucauld is content to paint the age in which he lived. Here the clemency spoken of is nothing more than an expression of the policy of Anne of Austria. Rochefoucauld had sacrificed all to her; even the favour of Cardinal Richelieu, but when she became regent she bestowed her favours upon those she hated; her friends were forgotten.--Aime Martin. The reader will hereby see that the age in which the writer lived best interprets his maxims.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Moderation of the happy arises from calm of good fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The moderation of those who are happy arises from the calm which good fortune bestows upon their temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Moderation due to fear of exciting envy; desire to appear greater
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation is caused by the fear of exciting the envy and contempt which those merit who are intoxicated with their good fortune; it is a vain display of our strength of mind, and in short the moderation of men at their greatest height is only a desire to appear greater than their fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. We have sufficient strength to support the misfortunes of others
rubrics_metrics.description: We have all sufficient strength to support the misfortunes of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The strongest example of this is the passage in Lucretius, lib. ii., line I:-- "Suave mari magno turbantibus aequora ventis E terra magnum alterius spectare laborem."]

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Constancy of the wise is concealment of agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The constancy of the wise is only the talent of concealing the agitation of their hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [Thus wisdom is only hypocrisy, says a commentator. This definition of constancy is a result of maxim 18.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Condemned affect contempt for death which is fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are condemned to death affect sometimes a constancy and contempt for death which is only the fear of facing it; so that one may say that this constancy and contempt are to their mind what the bandage is to their eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [See this thought elaborated in maxim 504.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Philosophy triumphs over past and future evils, not present
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy triumphs easily over past evils and future evils; but present evils triumph over it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. Few know death; we endure it from determination, stupidity, custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Few people know death, we only endure it, usually from determination, and even from stupidity and custom; and most men only die because they know not how to prevent dying.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. Great men cast down by misfortune show ambition not mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When great men permit themselves to be cast down by the continuance of misfortune, they show us that they were only sustained by ambition, and not by their mind; so that PLUS a great vanity, heroes are made like other men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [Both these maxims have been rewritten and made conciser by the author; the variations are not worth quoting.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. Greater virtues required to sustain good than evil fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: We need greater virtues to sustain good than evil fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Prosperity do{th} best discover vice, but adversity do{th} best discover virtue."--Lord Bacon, Essays{, (1625), "Of Adversity"}.] {The quotation wrongly had "does" for "doth".}

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Neither the sun nor death can be looked at without winking
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the sun nor death can be looked at without winking.

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. People vain of passions; envy too timid to avow
rubrics_metrics.description: People are often vain of their passions, even of the worst, but envy is a passion so timid and shame-faced that no one ever dare avow her.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. Jealousy is just and reasonable; envy is a fury
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is in a manner just and reasonable, as it tends to preserve a good which belongs, or which we believe belongs to us, on the other hand envy is a fury which cannot endure the happiness of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Evil we do attracts less hatred than our good qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The evil that we do does not attract to us so much persecution and hatred as our good qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. We have more strength than will; 'impossible' often excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: We have more strength than will; and it is often merely for an excuse we say things are impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. If no faults we would not delight in noting others'
rubrics_metrics.description: If we had no faults we should not take so much pleasure in noting those of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. Jealousy lives on doubt; ends or rages when doubt ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy lives upon doubt; and comes to an end or becomes a fury as soon as it passes from doubt to certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Pride indemnifies itself and loses nothing when casting away vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride indemnifies itself and loses nothing even when it casts away vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [See maxim 450, where the author states, what we take from our other faults we add to our pride.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. Without pride we would not complain of others' pride
rubrics_metrics.description: If we had no pride we should not complain of that of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["The proud are ever most provoked by pride."--Cowper, Conversation 160.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. Pride similar in all men; differs in manner of showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride is much the same in all men, the only difference is the method and manner of showing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Pride bestowed on all a common friend."--Pope, Essay On Man, Ep. ii., line 273.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. Nature gave pride to spare mortification from imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: It would seem that nature, which has so wisely ordered the organs of our body for our happiness, has also given us pride to spare us the mortification of knowing our imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Pride dominates remonstrances; we reprove to show our freedom from faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride has a larger part than goodness in our remonstrances with those who commit faults, and we reprove them not so much to correct as to persuade them that we ourselves are free from faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. We promise according to hopes; perform according to fears
rubrics_metrics.description: We promise according to our hopes; we perform according to our fears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["The reason why the Cardinal (Mazarin) deferred so long to grant the favours he had promised, was because he was persuaded that hope was much more capable of keeping men to their duty than gratitude."--Fragments Historiques. Racine.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 39. Interest plays all characters, even disinterestedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest speaks all sorts of tongues and plays all sorts of characters; even that of disinterestedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 40. Interest blinds some, makes some see
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest blinds some and makes some see.

rubrics_metrics.name: 41. Attention to little things makes one incapable of great things
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who apply themselves too closely to little things often become incapable of great things.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. Not enough strength to follow all our reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We have not enough strength to follow all our reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Man believes himself leader when he is led
rubrics_metrics.description: A man often believes himself leader when he is led; as his mind endeavours to reach one goal, his heart insensibly drags him towards another.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Strength/weakness of mind are arrangement of bodily organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength and weakness of mind are mis-named; they are really only the good or happy arrangement of our bodily organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Temper caprice more whimsical than Fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The caprice of our temper is even more whimsical than that of Fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Philosophers' attachment/indifference to life is style of self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: The attachment or indifference which philosophers have shown to life is only the style of their self love, about which we can no more dispute than of that of the palate or of the choice of colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Our temper sets price upon every gift from fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Our temper sets a price upon every gift that we receive from fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Happiness in taste not things themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is in the taste, and not in the things themselves; we are happy from possessing what we like, not from possessing what others like.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. We are never so happy or unhappy as we suppose
rubrics_metrics.description: We are never so happy or so unhappy as we suppose.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Those thinking they have merit persuade themselves they are honoured by being unhappy
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who think they have merit persuade themselves that they are honoured by being unhappy, in order to persuade others and themselves that they are worthy to be the butt of fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Ambition has been so strong as to make very miserable men take comfort that they were supreme in misery; and certain it is{, that where} we cannot distinguish ourselves by something excellent, we begin to take a complacency in some singular infirmities, follies, or defects of one kind or other." --Burke, {On The Sublime And Beautiful, (1756), Part I, Sect. XVII}.] {The translators' incorrectly cite Speech On Conciliation With America. Also, Burke does not actually write "Ambition has been...", he writes "It has been..." when speaking of ambition.}

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Satisfaction diminished by seeing our changeable approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing should so much diminish the satisfaction which we feel with ourselves as seeing that we disapprove at one time of that which we approve of at another.

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Compensation of good and evil renders fortunes equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever difference there appears in our fortunes, there is nevertheless a certain compensation of good and evil which renders them equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Nature and fortune together make the hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever great advantages nature may give, it is not she alone, but fortune also that makes the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Philosophers' contempt of riches is a hidden desire to avenge merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The contempt of riches in philosophers was only a hidden desire to avenge their merit upon the injustice of fortune, by despising the very goods of which fortune had deprived them; it was a secret to guard themselves against the degradation of poverty, it was a back way by which to arrive at that distinction which they could not gain by riches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["It is always easy as well as agreeable for the inferior ranks of mankind to claim merit from the contempt of that pomp and pleasure which fortune has placed beyond their reach. The virtue of the primitive Christians, like that of the first Romans, was very frequently guarded by poverty and ignorance."--Gibbon, Decline And Fall, Chap. 15.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Hate of favourites is love of favour (envy disguised)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hate of favourites is only a love of favour. The envy of NOT possessing it, consoles and softens its regrets by the contempt it evinces for those who possess it, and we refuse them our homage, not being able to detract from them what attracts that of the rest of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. We do everything to appear established to establish ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish ourselves in the world we do everything to appear as if we were established.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Great actions often result of chance not design
rubrics_metrics.description: Although men flatter themselves with their great actions, they are not so often the result of a great design as of chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Our actions have lucky/unlucky stars influencing blame/praise
rubrics_metrics.description: It would seem that our actions have lucky or unlucky stars to which they owe a great part of the blame or praise which is given them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Skilful men draw advantage from misfortune; foolish men harm from fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no accidents so unfortunate from which skilful men will not draw some advantage, nor so fortunate that foolish men will not turn them to their hurt.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Fortune turns all things to advantage of those she favours
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune turns all things to the advantage of those on whom she smiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Happiness depends on dispositions as well as fortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: The happiness or unhappiness of men depends no less upon their dispositions than their fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Still to ourselves in every place consigned Our own felicity we make or find." Goldsmith, Traveller, 431.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Sincerity is openness of heart; rare, often artful dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is an openness of heart; we find it in very few people; what we usually see is only an artful dissimulation to win the confidence of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Aversion to lying often hidden ambition for credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The aversion to lying is often a hidden ambition to render our words credible and weighty, and to attach a religious aspect to our conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Truth does less good than counterfeits do evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth does not do as much good in the world, as its counterfeits do evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Prudence lavished praise but cannot assure trifling event
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no praise we have not lavished upon Prudence; and yet she cannot assure to us the most trifling event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The author corrected this maxim several times, in 1665 it is No. 75; 1666, No. 66; 1671-5, No. 65; in the last edition it stands as at present. In the first he quotes Juvenal, Sat. X., line 315. " Nullum numen habes si sit Prudentia, nos te; Nos facimus, Fortuna, deam, coeloque locamus."]

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Clever man should regulate interests in due order; greediness troubles
rubrics_metrics.description: A clever man ought to so regulate his interests that each will fall in due order. Our greediness so often troubles us, making us run after so many things at the same time, that while we too eagerly look after the least we miss the greatest.

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Good sense to mind as grace is to body
rubrics_metrics.description: What grace is to the body good sense is to the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Love is desire to rule in soul; sympathy in mind; wish to possess in body
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to define love; all we can say is, that in the soul it is a desire to rule, in the mind it is a sympathy, and in the body it is a hidden and delicate wish to possess what we love--Plus many mysteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Love is the love of one {singularly,} with desire to be singularly beloved."--Hobbes{Leviathan, (1651), Part I, Chapter VI}.] {Two notes about this quotation: (1) the translators' mistakenly have "singularity" for the first "singularly" and (2) Hobbes does not actually write "Love is the..."--he writes "Love of one..." under the heading "The passion of Love."}

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. Pure love if exists is concealed even from ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a pure love, exempt from the mixture of our other passions, it is that which is concealed at the bottom of the heart and of which even ourselves are ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. No disguise can long hide love or feign it where it does not exist
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Few ashamed of being beloved when they love no longer
rubrics_metrics.description: There are few people who would not be ashamed of being beloved when they love no longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Judged by majority of results love resembles hatred more than friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: If we judge of love by the majority of its results it rather resembles hatred than friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Few women never intrigued; rare to have intrigued only once
rubrics_metrics.description: We may find women who have never indulged in an intrigue, but it is rare to find those who have intrigued but once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Yet there are some, they say, who have had None}; But those who have, ne'er end with only one}."] {--Lord Byron, }Don Juan, {Canto} iii., stanza 4.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Only one sort of love but a thousand copies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is only one sort of love, but there are a thousand different copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Love and fire need perpetual motion; cease when hope/fear ceases
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither love nor fire can subsist without perpetual motion; both cease to live so soon as they cease to hope, or to fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [So Lord Byron{Stanzas, (1819), stanza 3} says of Love-- "Like chiefs of faction, His life is action."]

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Real love rare as real ghosts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is real love just as there are real ghosts; every person speaks of it, few persons have seen it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Oh Love! no habitant of earth thou art-- An unseen seraph, we believe in thee-- A faith whose martyrs are the broken heart,-- But never yet hath seen, nor e'er shall see The naked eye, thy form as it should be." {--Lord Byron, }Childe Harold, {Canto} iv., stanza 121.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. 'Love' name attributed to many engagements with which it has no concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Love lends its name to an infinite number of engagements (Commerces) which are attributed to it, but with which it has no more concern than the Doge has with all that is done in Venice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Love of justice often fear of suffering injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of justice is simply in the majority of men the fear of suffering injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Silence best for him who distrusts himself
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence is the best resolve for him who distrusts himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Changeability in friendship due to difficulty knowing soul's qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: What renders us so changeable in our friendship is, that it is difficult to know the qualities of the soul, but easy to know those of the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. We love what agrees with us; true friendship requires preference
rubrics_metrics.description: We can love nothing but what agrees with us, and we can only follow our taste or our pleasure when we prefer our friends to ourselves; nevertheless it is only by that preference that friendship can be true and perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Reconciliation with enemies is desire to better condition or weariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconciliation with our enemies is but a desire to better our condition, a weariness of war, the fear of some unlucky accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["Thus terminated that famous war of the Fronde. The Duke de la Rochefoucauld desired peace because of his dangerous wounds and ruined castles, which had made him dread even worse events. On the other side the Queen, who had shown herself so ungrateful to her too ambitious friends, did not cease to feel the bitterness of their resentment. 'I wish,' said she, 'it were always night, because daylight shows me so many who have betrayed me.'"--Memoires De Madame De Motteville, Tom. IV., p. 60. Another proof that although these maxims are in some cases of universal application, they were based entirely on the experience of the age in which the author lived.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Friendship is partnership of reciprocal interests
rubrics_metrics.description: What men term friendship is merely a partnership with a collection of reciprocal interests, and an exchange of favours--in fact it is but a trade in which self love always expects to gain something.

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. More disgraceful to distrust than to be deceived by friends
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more disgraceful to distrust than to be deceived by our friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. We persuade ourselves to love powerful people; interest produces friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: We often persuade ourselves to love people who are more powerful than we are, yet interest alone produces our friendship; we do not give our hearts away for the good we wish to do, but for that we expect to receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Our distrust of another justifies his deceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Our distrust of another justifies his deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Men would not live long in society were they not dupes of each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Men would not live long in society were they not the dupes of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [A maxim, adds Aime Martin, "Which may enter into the code of a vulgar rogue, but one is astonished to find it in a moral treatise." Yet we have scriptural authority for it: "Deceiving and being deceived."--2 TIM. iii. 13.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Self love alters estimation of friends' qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Self love increases or diminishes for us the good qualities of our friends, in proportion to the satisfaction we feel with them, and we judge of their merit by the manner in which they act towards us.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Everyone blames his memory, no one blames his judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone blames his memory, no one blames his judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. In life we please more by faults than good qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: In the intercourse of life, we please more by our faults than by our good qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Largest ambition least appearance when object impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest ambition has the least appearance of ambition when it meets with an absolute impossibility in compassing its object.

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Awakening a deceived man as to his merit does him a bad turn
rubrics_metrics.description: To awaken a man who is deceived as to his own merit is to do him as bad a turn as that done to the Athenian madman who was happy in believing that all the ships touching at the port belonged to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [That is, they cured him. The madman was Thrasyllus, son of Pythodorus. His brother Crito cured him, when he infinitely regretted the time of his more pleasant madness.--See Aelian, Var. Hist. iv. 25. So Horace-- ------------"Pol, me occidistis, amici, Non servastis," ait, "cui sic extorta voluptas Et demptus per vim mentis gratissimus error." HOR. EP. ii--2, 138, of the madman who was cured of a pleasant lunacy.]

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Old men give good advice as consolation for no longer setting bad examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Old men delight in giving good advice as a consolation for the fact that they can no longer set bad examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Great names degrade those who cannot sustain them
rubrics_metrics.description: Great names degrade instead of elevating those who know not how to sustain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Test of extraordinary merit: those who envy it most obliged to praise it
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of extraordinary merit is to see those who envy it the most yet obliged to praise it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. A man perhaps ungrateful but often less chargeable than benefactor
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is perhaps ungrateful, but often less chargeable with ingratitude than his benefactor is.

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Mind and judgment not different; judgment is light of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: We are deceived if we think that mind and judgment are two different matters: judgment is but the extent of the light of the mind. This light penetrates to the bottom of matters; it remarks all that can be remarked, and perceives what appears imperceptible. Therefore we must agree that it is the extent of the light in the mind that produces all the effects which we attribute to judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Everyone praises his heart, none dare praise understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone praises his heart, none dare praise their understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Politeness of mind consists in thinking chaste and refined thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Politeness of mind consists in thinking chaste and refined thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Gallantry of mind is saying empty things agreeably
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallantry of mind is saying the most empty things in an agreeable manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. Ideas often flash more complete than after much labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas often flash across our minds more complete than we could make them after much labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. The head ever the dupe of the heart
rubrics_metrics.description: The head is ever the dupe of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [A feeble imitation of that great thought "All folly comes from the heart."--Aime Martin. But Bonhome, in his L'art De Penser, says "Plusieurs diraient en periode quarre que quelques reflexions que fasse l'esprit et quelques resolutions qu'il prenne pour corriger ses travers le premier sentiment du coeur renverse tous ses projets. Mais il n'appartient qu'a M. de la Rochefoucauld de dire tout en un mot que l'esprit est toujours la dupe du coeur."]

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. Knowing one's mind not same as knowing one's heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who know their minds do not necessarily know their hearts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Men and things have proper perspective; some judged near, others at distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Men and things have each their proper perspective; to judge rightly of some it is necessary to see them near, of others we can never judge rightly but at a distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. Accidentally discovering sense not rational; rational one understands and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: A man for whom accident discovers sense, is not a rational being. A man only is so who understands, who distinguishes, who tests it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. To understand rightly we should understand details; knowledge superficial
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand matters rightly we should understand their details, and as that knowledge is almost infinite, our knowledge is always superficial and imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. One kind of flirtation is to boast we never flirt
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind of flirtation is to boast we never flirt.

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Head cannot play part of heart long
rubrics_metrics.description: The head cannot long play the part of the heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Youth changes tastes by warmth; age retains tastes by habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth changes its tastes by the warmth of its blood, age retains its tastes by habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. Nothing is given so profusely as advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is given so profusely as advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. More we love a woman the more prone we are to hate her
rubrics_metrics.description: The more we love a woman the more prone we are to hate her.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. Blemishes of mind increase by age like those of face
rubrics_metrics.description: The blemishes of the mind, like those of the face, increase by age.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. There may be good but no pleasant marriages
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be good but there are no pleasant marriages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Inconsolable at deception by enemies and betrayal by friends; often content to be served by ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: We are inconsolable at being deceived by our enemies and betrayed by our friends, yet still we are often content to be thus served by ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. As easy to deceive oneself as to deceive others
rubrics_metrics.description: It is as easy unwittingly to deceive oneself as to deceive others.

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Asking/giving advice insincere; giver gains reputation or interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is less sincere than the way of asking and giving advice. The person asking seems to pay deference to the opinion of his friend, while thinking in reality of making his friend approve his opinion and be responsible for his conduct. The person giving the advice returns the confidence placed in him by eager and disinterested zeal, in doing which he is usually guided only by his own interest or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ["I have often thought how ill-natured a maxim it was which on many occasions I have heard from people of good understanding, 'That as to what related to private conduct no one was ever the better for advice.' But upon further examination I have resolved with myself that the maxim might be admitted without any violent prejudice to mankind. For in the manner advice was generally given there was no reason I thought to wonder it should be so ill received, something there was which strangely inverted the case, and made the giver to be the only gainer. For by what I could observe in many occurrences of our lives, that which we called giving advice was properly taking an occasion to show our own wisdom at another's expense."]
